title: Neurochemical & Behavioral Correlates of ETOH Effects
text:
This training program directly addresses the great need for highly trained scientists in an area of public health
urgency – alcoholism, the consequences of which are devastating to the individual or developing fetus as in the
case of fetal alcohol spectrum disorders. Trainees will learn cutting edge research techniques and will perform
research on alcohol related problems to provide new information that may guide treatments or further our
understanding of the causes and consequences of the disease of alcoholism.

title: Project 1 - Immunologic and Cellular Mechanisms of T1D Modifier Mutations
text: The goal of Project 1 is to understand in detail the pathological consequences of ENU-induced mutations implicated by Core B and Core C to modify the T1D phenotype of NOD/NckH mice, and to determine the cellular mechanisms by which those mutations impact the development of T1D. As we have done for Dusp10, a spontaneous mutation bred to homozygosity in our lab based on phenotypic selection, we will analyze each selected mutation to determine which salient immunopathological steps—recognized as hallmarks of T1D initiation and/or progression—are affected. To that end, we will use tools such as analysis of pancreatic islet infiltration (i.e. insulitis); measurement of the numbers and the in vivo functional capacity in various lymphoid organs of diabetogenic or regulatory CD4+FoxP3+ T lymphocytes; and analysis of islet antigen presentation using adoptive transfer of diabetogenic cells expressing the transgenic BDC2.5 T cell receptor (specific for an autoantigenic fusion peptide incorporating insulin and chromogranin A sequences) into 4-week-old recipients. We will pay particular attention to mechanisms of insulin resistance, and to the definition of markers of increased β-cell sensitivity witnessed with particular genetic mutations. In doing so it is plausible that novel immunopathological steps will be discovered. Second, we will investigate the contribution of particular tissues or cell types bearing each mutation to the development of T1D using bone marrow transplantation, adoptive transfer in neonates, islet transplantation, tissue-specific conditional knockout mice, and islet organoid cultures in the presence or absence of immune cells. Results will provide important guidance to Project 2, focused on molecular pathogenesis. We will perform cellular mechanistic studies to understand of the effects of mutations in Paqr8 (protective), and Dusp10, Rapgef1, and Xpnpep1 (exacerbating), identified in our initial collaboration. We expect to actively pursue mechanistic studies of four to six proteins at a time, adding one new protein per year by mutual agreement with Project 2. We expect that strong synergy between Projects will accelerate our progress. An important question we will address is the relevance of our findings to human health. To understand how mutations identified in NOD mice relate to human T1D, we will study the effects of selected mutations in NOD mice bearing a T1D-susceptible humanized immune system modified to contain or lack the orthologous mutations in human hematopoietic stem cells and/or human islet cells. We will also identify human T1D patients with mutations in genes orthologous to those we implicated in our screen of NOD mice. Our findings will uncover new therapeutic targets for treatment of T1D and help to improve prediction of T1D onset in humans.

title: Project 2: Orexin Signaling and Hypoventilation
text: This Project focuses on improving breathing in mouse models of Obesity Hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) and Opioid-Induced Respiratory Depression (OIRD) as these disorders are relatively common causes of hypoventilation and have very high mortality. OHS occurs in people with severe obesity and is manifest as hypoventilation during wakefulness and especially during sleep. Opiates also reduce ventilation, and about 6% of Americans take prescription opioids which can cause hypoventilation and worsen sleep apnea and other respiratory disorders. Considering these staggering impacts, there is a large and unmet need to develop better therapies for these hypoventilation disorders. Several lines of evidence indicate that increasing orexin signaling through the orexin receptors should be a highly effective therapy for people with OHS and OIRD. The orexin neurons excite all key brainstem regions regulating ventilation. In addition, orexin knockout mice have a blunted response to hypercarbia, and orexin receptor antagonists reduce the response to hypercarbia. We hypothesize that increased activity of the orexin neurons and orexin agonists will improve breathing in mouse models of OHS and OIRD via lower brainstem respiratory circuits. As a model of OHS, we will use mice with diet-induced obesity which are severely obese and have hypoventilation with a reduced hypercapnic ventilatory response. In addition, we will study mice treated with morphine as a model of OIRD. These Aims seek to determine the role of orexin signaling in the responses to hypercapnia and OIRD. This Project synergizes well with Projects 1, 3, and 4 that seek to enhance ventilatory responses to hypercapnia and OIRD in mice, and Project 5 which seeks to identify pharmacological methods to improve hypoventilation in people, especially with OIRD. The first Aim is to determine if the orexin neurons are necessary for the HCVR and OIRD with morphine in a novel mouse model. Second, we will define the location and molecular identity of orexin-responsive neurons in the brainstem using in situ hybridization, calcium imaging and RNAseq, in collaboration with the Electrophysiology and Molecular Biology Cores. The third Aim is to test if the orexin neurons are sufficient to improve the response to hypercapnia and OIRD. Finally, we will test of an orexin agonist improves the HCVR and OIRD and then map the brainstem regions through which this occurs. Collectively, these experiments should demonstrate that orexin signaling improves hypoventilation in mouse models of OHS and OIRD, and that orexin agonists have potential for improving these disorders.

title: Hands-on Education and Research for Biomedical and Analytical Learning (HERBAL)
text:
The University of Rhode Island proposes the development of a new program to cultivate STEM learning for high
school students. This program – HERBAL: Hands-on Education and Research for Biomedical and Analytical
Learning – is composed of teacher training workshops followed by an academic year laboratory paired with
game-based learning modules centered on molecules from medicinal plants. The academic year course will be
followed by hands-on summer research with student-generated data at the University of Rhode Island. The
HERBAL program will serve as an excellent entry point for life-long STEM learning, and it will connect plants
with their cultural and traditional importance to human health and well-being, and HERBAL will increase student
access to cutting-edge analysis and informatics tools to understand the metabolite composition of these plants.

title: Computational rational design of carbohydrate and nucleic acid drug scaffolds with multiscale dynamics and AI
text:
Drug discovery is expensive and time consuming, and applying computer-based rational design in the early
stages can accelerate the process and lower costs. However, computational investigations of
carbohydrates, nucleic acids and fluorescent molecules are challenging to simulate without inclusion of
complex physics. This proposal aims to combine simulations, high quality automated database generation,
and the development of machine learning models in order to understand the binding and behavior of
carbohydrate-based heparanase inhibitors as possible anti-cancer drug targets, and the photophysical
behavior and connection to structure for fluorescent nucleic acids.

title: CRCNS: Deep Learning to Discover Neurovascular Disruptions in Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Knowledge of critical interactions among various brain cells is central to understanding the underlying causes of age-related cognitive decline as well as Alzheimer’s dementia. However, accurate identification of molecular changes in 
these cells is hard to accomplish using conventional methods. The current project will develop advanced deep learning 
methods and techniques to elucidate pathological mechanisms leading to Alzheimer’s disease, which will enable the 
identification of novel biomarkers and treatment strategies.

title: Overcoming pre-existing immunity to AAV to enhance AAV-based HIV immunotherapies
text:
Despite the promise of adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated delivery of anti-HIV biologics for
preventing and treating HIV infection, translating this approach to the clinic is hindered by the high prevalence
of anti-AAV neutralizing (n) antibodies (Abs) in humans. To tackle this barrier, we will identify the least prevalent
AAV serotypes in people living with HIV in the epicenter of the HIV/AIDS epidemic and assess whether depletion
of circulating IgG molecules can reduce pre-existing anti-AAV Ab levels sufficiently to allow AAV-mediated
delivery of anti-HIV biologics to nonhuman primates. If successful, this research could bring us closer to testing
the efficacy of AAV-based immunotherapies in people, regardless of their AAV serostatus.

title: Role of the PilC1 and PilC2 pilus-associated proteins in Kingella kingae pathogenicity
text:
Kingella kingae has emerged as a leading cause of septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, sepsis, and other invasive
diseases in young children and is associated with significant short-term and long-term morbidity. Reports that
an increasing percentage of K. kingae isolates are resistant to -lactams and other antibiotics raise concern
about approaches to treatment in the future. The proposed studies will elucidate the central role of the PilC1
and PilC2 pilus-associated proteins in K. kingae type IV pili structure and function and will provide insights into
the design of novel therapeutics against K. kingae and other pathogens that produce type IV pili.

title: Human Neurogenesis: Unraveling Controversies and Charting New Frontiers
text:
This meeting will bring together leaders in the field of human hippocampal neurogenesis to review evidence,
discuss the ongoing dispute on the existence of neurogenesis in the human brain and advise on the most
effective approach to move the field forward.

title: Screening for protein interaction inhibitors of the ERKS axis for brain tumor treatment
text:
We propose to engineer specific small molecule inhibitors of the ERKS axis proteins, which are essential for the
proliferation of brain tumor stem/progenitor cells. Small molecule inhibitors developed from this project are
expected to provide potential therapeutics for brain tumor treatment.

title: Impact of APOE deficiency on HPA axis function and cognition
text:
The hypomorphic E4 allele of APOE is the strongest genetic risk for Alzheimer's Disease, yet it is unclear how it
contributes to AD etiology. We propose to investigate the molecular consequences of APOE deficiency on the
HPA axis and their interaction on learning and memory.

title: HSP70 as an actionable cancer-specific target
text:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the most common form of pancreatic cancer, is a lethal malignancy
with no curative treatment options. This proposal leverages a newly developed HSP70 inhibitor with a unique
mechanism of action to investigate tumor cell-intrinsic and extrinsic pathways by which it attenuates PDAC. We
will also evaluate rational combination strategies to enhance the anti-tumor efficacy of HSP70 inhibition, with the
long-term goal of translating these findings into therapies that improve outcomes for patients with PDAC.

title: Core D- Data Science Core
text: BEAMS-2 Core D Asthma affects schoolchildren in Tucson at a higher rate than schoolchildren of the same ancestry living in nearby Nogales, Sonora, Mexico. In BEAMS-1, we showed that differences in prenatal and early-life exposures through their influence on gut microbiota, immune system development, and gene-environment interactions impact the risk of childhood asthma. Building on these findings, the Data Science Core (Core D) will support three BEAMS-2 Projects aimed at discovering protective exposures in Mexico and elucidating the biological mechanisms underlying asthma development. Core D comprises experienced qualitative scientists with deep expertise in pediatric asthma, cohort studies, and advanced methods for analyzing microbiome, transcriptomic, and single-cell data. Core D will support BEAMS-2 through three primary aims. First, the Core will provide biostatistics study design and rigorous quantitative analysis for all Projects, including epidemiological studies (P1), microbiome studies (P2), and mouse model studies (P3). Second, Core D will lead the application of statistical machine learning and bioinformatics methods for microbiome, metabolomics, transcriptomic, and single-cell data. Third, the Core will maintain and expand an integrated data management infrastructure to support BEAMS-2, ensuring data quality and reproducibility while enabling secure data sharing across all Projects and Cores. As a central component of the PPG, Core D works closely with each Project, the Administrative Core, and the Program Leader to align biostatistics, bioinformatics, and data management efforts with both individual investigator needs and the program’s overarching scientific goals.

title: Biomaterial-directed patterning of xenografted brain organoids in-vivo
text:
Modeling the human brain with accuracy and reliability remains a key challenge in the field of neuroscience
and is the basis for our understanding of prevalent diseases such as Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, epilepsy, and
others. My dissertation project aims to improve a new type of model – xenotransplantation of human brain
organoids into rodent cortex – by directing cell patterning and neuronal circuit integration into host systems.
Results from this project will establish improved, human-centric models of brain development and contribute to
our collective understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying human brain development.

title: Epigenomic Control of KSHV Latency
text:
The long-term goal of this R01 is to further advance our knowledge of the AIDS-defining malignancies caused
by Kaposi’s Sarcoma-Associated Herpesvirus (KSHV). Investigation of the mechanisms regulating KSHV
latency, episome persistence and oncogenesis through a deeper understanding of KSHV LANA will provide
novel viral-specific targets for therapeutic intervention in KSHV-associated cancers and related disorders.

title: Multimodal Assessment of Near-term Risk Processes for Suicidal Ideation and Behavior
text:
Suicide is a major public health issue and ranks within the top 9 leading causes of death in adults aged 18 to
64. This research will contribute to our ability to better predict acute increases in suicidal ideation and
transitions to suicide attempts in the near term, having direct implications for suicide risk assessment, risk
stratification, and personalized intervention approaches aimed at reducing and preventing suicide.

title: Dynamic Haptic Robotic Training for Central Venous Catheter Insertion
text:
The goal of this study is to develop and assess the impact of advanced technologies of Resident Artificial
Intelligent Skills Education (R[AI]SE) and R[AI]SE with augmented reality (R[AI]SEAR) have on resident
cognitive and psychomotor learning in performing Central Venous Catheterization (CVC) through a multi-
institutional study with Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, Hershey Medical Center, and West Virginia University
Medicine. Novel medical education training technologies will be developed and validated utilizing artificial
intelligence and augmented reality. Knowledge gained from this project will lead to enhanced medical training
that greatly improves patient health, reducing mechanical and infectious complications in CVC.

title: A community resource for germline and somatic genetic disease modeling in zebrafish
text:
Human genetic studies have produced hundreds of thousands of loci and candidate genes for a wide range of
diseases, but often have not resulted in sufficient mechanistic insight to lead to actionable changes in prevention,
diagnosis, or treatment. One of the rate-limiting steps has been animal modeling which is typically not feasible
at a large enough scale in animals closely related to humans, though in recent years the zebrafish has begun to
fill this gap. We have created, maintained and continued to develop a Zebrafish Community Resource to bring
state of the art technologies and disease modeling to investigators studying human disease.

title: Chronic nicotine effects on vulnerable brainstem neurons
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it examines the effects on chronic nicotine on the
midbrain and brainstem neurons that are particularly vulnerable to neurodegeneration in Parkinson’s Disease.
Thus, the proposed research is relevant to the mission of NIH because it will create fundamental mechanistic
knowledge about the effects of nicotine that can be used to develop novel targets for the prevention of
Parkinson’s Disease in high-risk individuals. This research will help reduce the burden of neurological disease
because it is the first step in developing non-toxic and non-addictive therapeutics that could slow the
progression of neuropathology in the earliest stages of Parkinson’s disease.

title: Improving Sepsis Care with Deep RNA Sequencing Data
text:
Sepsis is responsible for one out of five deaths worldwide. We propose to use RNA sequencing data to
improve the diagnosis and treatment of sepsis in immune suppressed patients (cancer and kidney transplant)
through pathogen identification and improved understanding of RNA biology.
